title: Reorder Data in Log Files
statement:
Each string in `logs` is a log: words separated by single spaces, where the first word is the log's identifier and everything after the first space is its content. Every log is one of two kinds:

- a **letter-log**, whose content words are all made of lowercase English letters;
- a **digit-log**, whose content words are all made of digits.

Return the logs rearranged so that all letter-logs come first, ordered by their content compared lexicographically as whole strings; letter-logs with equal content are ordered by identifier, also lexicographically. All digit-logs follow, in the same relative order they had in `logs`.
constraints: Words in logs[i] are separated by exactly one space
Each log has an identifier and at least one word after it
Identifiers use lowercase letters and digits
notes:
## Intuition

The two kinds of logs follow different rules: digit-logs keep their order, letter-logs are sorted. So separate them first, sort only the letter-logs with a two-level key (content, then identifier), and glue the digit-logs on the end unchanged. A single sort with a clever comparator also works, but it must be stable and treat every pair of digit-logs as equal, which is easy to get wrong.

## Approach

1. Make two lists, `letterLogs` and `digitLogs`.
2. For each `log`, find the first `space`; the part before it is `id`, the part after it is `content`.
3. All content words share a kind, so the first character of `content` decides it: a digit sends the whole log to `digitLogs`, otherwise `{ id, content, log }` goes to `letterLogs`.
4. Sort `letterLogs` by `content`, and by `id` when contents are equal.
5. Return the sorted letter-logs followed by `digitLogs` in their original order.

## Example 1, step by step

`logs = ["dig1 8 1 5 1", "let1 art can", "dig2 3 6", "let2 own kit dig", "let3 art zero"]`.

- `digitLogs` gets `"dig1 8 1 5 1"` and `"dig2 3 6"`, in that order.
- `letterLogs` gets contents `"art can"` (let1), `"own kit dig"` (let2) and `"art zero"` (let3).
- Sorting the contents gives `"art can"` < `"art zero"` < `"own kit dig"`.

The answer is `["let1 art can", "let3 art zero", "let2 own kit dig", "dig1 8 1 5 1", "dig2 3 6"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L · n log n), where n is the number of logs and L their length: each comparison may scan a whole content string.
- Space: O(n · L) for the split lists and the copied contents.

## Pitfalls

- Split at the **first** space only; the content keeps its inner spaces and is compared as one string, so `"ar t"` comes before `"art"`.
- Identical contents must fall back to the identifier: `"a1 art can"` comes before `"b2 art can"`.
- Identifiers may contain digits too, so classify a log by its content, never by its first character.
- Do not sort the digit-logs at all; their input order is the answer.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `letterLogs` | letter-logs as `{ id, content, log }` records |
| `digitLogs` | digit-logs in input order |
| `space` | index of the first space in `log` |
| `id`, `content` | the identifier and everything after it |
| `isDigit` | whether the content starts with a digit |
| `sorted` | the letter-logs' original strings after sorting |
